anchor: Paul Klee, Pedagogical Sketchbook (Bauhausbuch 2, 1925; Praeger 1953), the model the 2023 application names for itself ('Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook in drag, in VR'), for the macro-order, checked against the Praeger text (work/klee_ps.txt); Kandinsky, Point and Line to Plane (1926) for Part I; Albers, Interaction of Color (1963) for the method of every ARGUMENT; Nake, Nees and Molnar (1965-74) for where chance enters. Grafted from Form+Code in Design, Art, and Architecture (Reas, McWilliams, LUST, 2010): its five verbs (Repeat, Transform, Parameterize, Visualize, Simulate) as navigation handles on every chapter and Parameterize as a part of its own; from Code as Creative Medium (Levin and Brain, 2021): the brief with precedent, closed exercise and open make, and three of its assignments.
title: The Sketchbook in Drag, Parameterized: point, line, plane, family, balance, fall, swing, colour, and out
thesis: This course walks the way Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook walks, the book Ada's own research plan says it wants to put 'in drag, in VR'. A point goes for a walk and becomes a line; the line closes into a plane you can stand on; the plane repeats and becomes structure; chance disturbs the structure and, given a memory, becomes ground; the body gets joints, becomes a family, stands, falls along a curve, swings, sounds and glows, and the book ends in colour. Where Klee stops, the course follows Ada's spine out of the sketchbook and says so. Every chapter also carries one of five verbs (repeat, transform, parameterize, visualize, simulate), so you can always say what your code is doing to form, and each verb needs the one before it: disorder is invisible without a grid, a family needs a class, a simulation needs all of these. The programming ideas arrive when a body needs them: a point needs a variable, a line a function, a walk a list, a floor a loop, a family a class, a balance physics, a curve your own gravity, a swing sine. In every chapter you build a body in GDScript, vary it along one axis, write down before rendering which two variants will look most alike, defend one sentence with the picture, ask what the approximation owes or hides, and then stand on the body, carry it, walk through it or become it. 'In drag' is not a costume here: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, tendon and bone and onto male and female, and the scene tree does the same with parent and child. You will learn that hierarchy, and then make the passive end drive.

parts.title: Point, line, plane (Kandinsky; Klee I.1-4)
parts.promise: From a point you place to a plane you walked and can stand on, and a first build that runs outside your editor. You learn that the engine calls your code, that everything is an object in a tree, that a line is a record of a walk, and that a machine drafter fills your gaps with its defaults.

parts.title: Structure: repetition, disorder, articulation (Klee I.5-12; Nake, Nees, Molnar)
parts.promise: Repeat a body and it becomes a floor; move the rule into the surface and it becomes a pattern; disturb it and chance appears; give chance a memory and it becomes ground you can walk; articulate the body and it moves by itself.

parts.title: The family (Klee I.7-8; Albers; Molnar): Parameterize, declared as an addition
parts.promise: You describe a body in a single class whose exported fields make a family, sweep one axis into a comparison sheet, measure what each value costs, save a body as a file, and bring a found body into the family's room. The short track pivots into its mini project here.

parts.title: Dimension and balance (Klee II)
parts.promise: The eye and the standing body: perspective as a fact about eye height, balance as a fact about the centre of mass, and legs that let the passive end drive. The walker you have used since day one is opened.

parts.title: The gravitational curve (Klee III)
parts.promise: You write gravity yourself: a curve from steps, regions with other laws, a stair that is a function, and a small complete game about staying upright.

parts.title: Kinetic and chromatic energy (Klee IV; Albers)
parts.promise: Motions that return: pendulum, circle, spiral, sound, the arrow and the field of arrows; then colour as a system and the shader. Each makes something invisible visible, and each picture hides a choice.

parts.title: Out of the sketchbook: bodies in drag (spine 13-25)
parts.promise: Where Klee has no page: rules in time, recursion that must be stopped, grammars, generated worlds, soft, implicit and collective bodies, bodies that learn, the crisis of foundations, entropy measured on your own predictions, and your hall in the collective museum.

tracks.title: Three weeks: the sketchbook's first page and one family (Queer 3D World format)
tracks.length: 3 weeks (15 days). Week 1 (Part I on the runnable kits, two chapters a day on days 1-3): ch01-ch08, with the first export on Friday and a scanning / Tilt Brush session whose results wait for ch18. Week 2: ch09, ch11, ch12, ch14, ch18 (export on Friday; the mini-project brief is due the same day as a flowchart and a paper prototype). Week 3: mini project, with two critique sessions in the SFPC Code Societies format and no new code: (a) Klee's active/passive passage and the scene tree's command chain, walked as encounters in Trans_Body and VFM_09_Legs; (b) the blob aesthetic and the default body, walked in ISO_Metaballs and ML_Classification. The class shows on day 15.
tracks.supplied: Named, not taught, each with the chapter where the long track opens it: the desktop walker and the XR rig (commons/scenes/vr_staging.tscn with Godot XR Tools; opened at ch19); the runnable kits in doc/book/studies/ (day-zero, point-zero, point-one with contact_probe.gd, point-coordinates, point-lines, point-trace, random-definition with display.gd); the SKETCH helper point(p), line(a, b), box(p, size), seeded by point-lines' segment.gd (opened at ch5); the sweep_sheet scene that lays out labelled members (to be written for the course; opened and rewritten at ch15); a heightfield-to-mesh-and-collider helper for ch12; pickables and a desktop carry; one AudioStreamPlayer3D sound; a phone-scan or Tilt Brush route to glTF through Blender; an export preset per machine. Skipped and covered by those parts: ch10 (pattern), ch13 (the organism: delta and pivots arrive inside the walker), ch15-17, and Parts IV-VII.
tracks.mini_project: A family in drag (prompts after Code as Creative Medium and Form+Code: Virtual Creature, Parametric Object, Extrapolated Body, Personal Prosthetic). One class of your own with one exported axis of 3-5 values; the closest pair predicted in writing before rendering; the comparison sheet; one claim sentence the sheet supports; one debt comment in the code saying what the approximation owes or hides; the members placed with your scanned or sculpted body in the walkable room of your ch18 build, where a visitor can stand on, walk through, carry or become one of them. Shown to the class as a desktop build and, where a headset is available, walked in VR.

tracks.title: One year: the whole sketchbook, parameterized, and out of it
tracks.length: About 36 teaching weeks. Part I runs at two chapters a week; after that about one chapter a week. Five syntheses (ch08, ch18, ch25 midterm, ch30, ch41 final) are each followed by a pause week with no new code (Aesthetic Programming's rhythm). The final project is planned at ch40, two units before the end, from the student's own prediction log.
tracks.mini_project: Midterm at ch25: a round in your room that a classmate can lose, exported and played. Final at ch41: your hall in Ada's endless museum, built from your families and exported to desktop and Quest; for each body a prediction, a comparison sheet, a claim and a debt comment, plus one public sculpture with a stated edit rule (NoC's Ecosystem Project turned into a museum room that others may revise).

chapters.title: Day Zero: the instruction is the work
chapters.body: A LeWitt location drawing turned into one body: in the supplied base.tscn (floor, camera, light, Label3D) you type one line that calls a supplied place_at(where), and a cube appears at 'corner', 'midpoint' or 'centre'; one print() writes your instruction to the Output panel.

argument.axis: wording of the instruction
argument.predict: 'midpoint' and 'centre' will look most alike from the fixed camera: on a square floor both land on the middle line, and they differ only if 'midpoint' is read as the midpoint of an edge, which is exactly the ambiguity. 'somewhere near the middle' will not run at all: the helper refuses an unknown word with an error.
argument.claim: An instruction a partner can interpret is not one the engine can run: ambiguity shows up as an error, not as a variation.

chapters.debt: LeWitt's drafters interpreted; the engine refuses. Literalness is the price of repeatability, the course's first debt. GDScript's English keywords are programming's default language (Marino on FLOW-MATIC), a cheap first question for Swedish-speaking students.

chapters.title: Point: a body with no size must be given one
chapters.body: A point built in _ready(): a MeshInstance3D whose SphereMesh radius is a variable, placed by setting its position property; then three points by hand, and a Label3D beside them that counts the frames the engine has called you for (Point Zero's frame counter).

argument.axis: point radius seen from 2 m
argument.predict: 0.01 and 0.05 will look most alike: at 2 m both subtend under 1.5 degrees, a few pixels, and read as dots. 1.0 stops being a point and reads as a body; 0.25 is the one that changes category as you walk.
argument.claim: A point is a relation between size and viewing distance: Kandinsky's point becomes a plane when it grows.

chapters.debt: Mathematically a point has no extent; to be seen it needs a mesh of hundreds of triangles. The engine can show a point only by lying about its size, the first approximation of the course. And the frame counter counts frames, not seconds: in a 90 Hz headset it runs 1.5 times faster than at 60 Hz on the desktop. The repair (delta) is held back to ch13 and named there.

chapters.title: Solid and ghost: one if decides what a body is
chapters.body: Point One's three stations rebuilt: a boolean solid decides, in one if, whether a sphere gets a collider, and a second number sets the collider's radius apart from the visible radius. You call the supplied make_solid() and make_ghost() before you open them; the kit's contact probe (pink feelers) runs through the stations.

argument.axis: collider radius as a fraction of the visible radius (still taken with the probe's feelers paused against each sphere)
argument.predict: The ghost and 0.5 will look most alike: in both the feeler has entered the visible sphere (it passes through the ghost and stops halfway inside the 0.5 sphere). 1.5 stops the feeler in mid-air before it touches the surface.
argument.claim: What you see and what stops you are separate properties: one if and one number decide what a body is for another body.

chapters.debt: A still cannot show collision without a witness: the argument needs a second body (the probe) to make the first one's solidity visible, and so do players. Invisible walls and walkable ghosts are the course's first uncanny, and the gap between collider and mesh is a decision every game hides.
chapters.place: Walk into each sphere with the walker: the ghost lets you through, 0.5 lets you sink in, 1.0 stops you at the skin, 1.5 stops you before you touch it.

chapters.body: A segment between two carried points: your function show_between(a, b) places, scales and orients a thin box and returns the distance; a do-not-cross barrier reacts when that distance falls below a threshold (condition before threshold).

chapters.title: The walk: a line is a record
chapters.body: A trace recorder: in _process the carried point appends its position to an array once it has moved further than a gate distance (list before append; condition before threshold), and a loop redraws the array as an ImmediateMesh line strip.

argument.axis: sampling gate
argument.predict: 0.01 and 0.05 will look most alike: both are below the width a hand-drawn curve shows at 2 m, so both read as continuous. 0.5 turns the walk into a polygon with visible corners.
argument.claim: A recorded line is a sampling decision: below a few centimetres the walk looks continuous; above it the corners become the drawing.

chapters.debt: Continuity is faked from a list. Memory is not free, so the trace must forget (a bounded array), and forgetting is a choice about which past counts.

chapters.body: Close the walk: the recorded points become a triangle fan through SurfaceTool, normals are generated, and a collider made from the mesh lets you stand on the plane you walked.

chapters.title: When things go wrong: the drafter is a machine
chapters.body: A cube from 8 corners and 12 triangles (Point_Animatedcube's body), drafted by an AI assistant from your written instruction under a protocol of three lines: what should change, what must not change, and one observation that would prove the code wrong. You run it, step through it with breakpoints until you find where its faces turn inside out, repair it, and export a desktop build.

argument.axis: how much the prompt fixes
values: measured ('0.5 m, resting on the floor')
located ('at the end of my walk, in Godot's clockwise winding')
argument.predict: vague and counted will look most alike: both come back as a default 1 m cube at the origin, and both are likely inside out, because the model's idea of a cube comes from engines that wind counter-clockwise. Only 'located' is right side out on the first try.
argument.claim: Where the prompt is open, the model fills in its defaults: the generated body shows the model's idea of a body and of an engine, not yours.

chapters.debt: Algorithmic enclosure and the default body: the assistant learned from other people's code and repeats its norms (a cube at the origin, a capsule player, OpenGL winding). Chun's 'sourcery': seeing generated source is not knowing what it does. A build is a second machine with its own errors (read-only res://, another refresh rate).
chapters.place: Run your exported build on a classmate's laptop, or on the headset where one is available (the headset is an export): the first time your room exists outside your editor, and you stand in it.

chapters.title: The chessboard: purely repetitive and therefore structural
chapters.body: A floor of cubes instanced from a PackedScene in a nested loop. Each cube gets a StandardMaterial3D made in code, coloured by a rule over (x, z): first two colours of your own, then a hue from the index, Color.from_hsv(float(x + z) / (2 * n), s, v).

argument.axis: rhythm rule over the same 8 x 8 cubes
argument.predict: The chessboard and the x % 3 stripes will look most alike from 6 m, where both read as texture. The hue ramp is the only floor with a direction; 'every cell alike' is the only one without rhythm.
argument.claim: Structure is the repetition rule, not the cube: the same 64 bodies make four different floors.

chapters.debt: The grid is the unexamined ground of 3D (editor grids, voxels, the frame buffer as a grid, after Gaboury); it is a choice, and the standing ruling holds that the first line did not need it. HSV promises equal steps of hue, and the eye does not see them as equal: the yellow band looks brighter and wider than the blue one.

chapters.title: Pattern: structure moves into the surface
chapters.body: A tile written pixel by pixel into an Image from a 4 x 4 source kept as a Dictionary recipe {size, source, rule}, wrapped as an ImageTexture and repeated over your floor by UV scale; one get_color(x, y) function per symmetry rule (Symmetry_Seventeen's p1, pm and pg).

argument.axis: wallpaper rule over one 4 x 4 source
argument.predict: pm and pg will look most alike: both keep one mirror direction, and the glide only shifts alternate rows by half a tile. p4 is the outlier, the only one without a single preferred direction.
argument.claim: The same sixteen pixels make four patterns: symmetry is a rule applied to a source, and the rule is what we see.

chapters.debt: Texture filtering and mipmaps blur the rule at a distance (nearest against linear); the seventeen wallpaper groups are a closed classification that the ornament traditions they describe never needed.

chapters.title: Disturbed order: chance enters the grid
chapters.body: Schotter as a floor: your chessboard of cubes rotated and displaced by a seeded RandomNumberGenerator, more with every row; and 10 PRINT as a walkable maze, one of two rotations per cell.

argument.axis: disorder amplitude (maximum rotation in the last row)
argument.predict: 0 and 5 will look most alike: 5 degrees moves a 1 m cube's corner about 6 cm, less than the gap between cubes, so the grid still reads. Somewhere between 5 and 20 it stops reading as a grid.
argument.claim: Randomness is visible only against a structure already built: the grid is what lets us see disorder.

chapters.debt: Computer randomness is pseudo-random: the same seed returns the same 'chance' (Random_Definition: a pattern that returns). Nake's question from Hommage a Paul Klee (1965): can a pseudo-random number stand in for the artist's intuition? And a seed is a promise of repeatability that someone else can use to reproduce you.

chapters.title: Noise: chance that remembers its neighbour
chapters.body: A small walkable terrain: FastNoiseLite sampled on a grid into a PackedFloat32Array of heights, multiplied by an edge envelope and emitted as an ArrayMesh with a collider made from it (Noise_Space_10's body). A supplied heightfield helper covers the mesh step in the short track.

argument.axis: where the heights come from, all at the same amplitude and grid
argument.predict: The sine and the Perlin terrain will look most alike from above at this frequency: both roll smoothly, and the sine is only too regular. randf() is the outlier, a field of spikes, because no vertex knows its neighbour.
argument.claim: Noise is randomness with a memory of its neighbour: only the sources that remember can be walked on.

chapters.debt: The blob aesthetic (Queer 3D 2024): smooth noise became CGI's look of the 'natural'. And the grid decides how much of the noise exists: octaves finer than the vertex spacing are computed and never seen. Queer 3D's overflow-rate comparison of noise types (Perlin 45, random 635, Voronoi 0, sine-curve space 3284) says the same with numbers.

chapters.title: The organism: bone, tendon, muscle
chapters.body: A limb of three segments as a parent-child chain with pivots, each joint turning by angle += speed * delta in _process: the course's first body that moves by itself. Beside it, Trans_Body's lattice loses cells where the limb passes.

argument.axis: where the pivot sits on each segment (same joint angles)
argument.predict: 'at the end' and 'at one third' will look most alike after 30 degrees: both bend like a finger. 'outside' makes the chain orbit instead of bend.
argument.claim: A body's motion is decided by where its joints are, not by what its parts look like.

chapters.debt: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, tendon and bone, and onto male and female organs ('Male organs (anthers), active'). The scene tree encodes the same command chain: the parent moves the child, never the reverse. That hierarchy is taught here and inverted in ch21. And frames are not time: speed per frame runs 1.5 times faster at the headset's 90 Hz than at 60 Hz; delta is the repair promised in ch2.

chapters.title: Families: one body in a single class
chapters.body: Describe a body in a single class: class_name with two typed @export fields (for a sphere, rings and segments; for your own body, whatever makes it) and a build() function that makes the mesh in _ready(). The supplied sweep sheet instances four members side by side, labelled.

argument.axis: sphere segments (rings = half)
argument.predict: 16 and 64 will look most alike at 2 m: the silhouette of 16 segments misses the true circle by 1 - cos(11.25 deg), about 2% of the radius. 4 is not a coarse sphere but another body, close to an octahedron.
argument.claim: Above about 16 segments a sphere stops paying visibly; below 8 it changes category: the class's integer decides which body you have.

chapters.debt: A class's fields decide which bodies are possible (the CCSWG prompt 'describe it in a single class', turned to a body): an int cannot have 3.5 segments, and no value of rings makes a torus. Polycount against smooth deformation, the application's topology question, enters here. And a typed set() refuses a wrong type in silence, so a sweep can publish four identical members and look finished (the Ada project's own science_screen case).

chapters.body: Your class with setters that rebuild on change, a rebuild() method, and @tool so the family changes live in the editor (Color_Context_Placed's chroma_stack with its @export_enum rule is the precedent). argument.predict: 0 and 0.25 will look most alike: both are upright pyramids, the apex still over the base. Past 1.0 the apex leaves the base and the body leans, first an oblique pyramid, then a blade.
argument.claim: One exported field can carry a body across a category of form: from monument to lean-to.

chapters.debt: The Inspector slider hides what each value costs and what it breaks. chapters.title: The budget: polycount measured, a claim tested
chapters.body: A parametric surface, the catenoid (u, v) -> point, with exported u_steps and v_steps; and Primitives_Portals' torus ring whose segments double while its gap to the true circle is printed and asserted.

argument.axis: u_steps of the catenoid
argument.predict: 48 and 96 will look most alike at 2 m: at 48 steps the chord misses the circle by 1 - cos(3.75 deg), about 0.2% of the radius, while 96 costs twice the triangles. The prediction is also written as a test: gap_to_circle(n) < 0.01 passes from n = 24 (0.86%) and fails at 12 (3.4%).
argument.claim: A parametric surface has a step count below which it is a different body and above which it is only cost: the test finds the first, the profiler the second.

chapters.debt: 'Smooth' is a budget decision (application l.89: polycount against deforming a body smoothly), and in a headset at 72-90 Hz every triangle is drawn once per eye. A green test is a fact about the question you asked, not about the body (Montfort: valid and intentional are different).

argument.claim: Standing is a fact about the centre of mass and the support polygon, not about how heavy or large the body looks.

chapters.title: To stand despite all possibilities to fall: a round
chapters.body: A small complete game: stones that stand or sink on seeded random waits with a telegraphing ring (Random_Game's body), and the player crossing them. An enum state machine per stone (STANDING, WARNING, SINKING, GONE) and for the round (MENU, PLAYING, FALLEN, WON); a HUD with the time; the best time saved; a supplied sound on each sink (opened at ch27).

argument.axis: warning time before a stone sinks (still 20 s into the same seeded round)
argument.predict: 1.0 and 2.0 will look most alike: most stones are still standing and the gaps are few. At 0.25 s the field is mostly gaps, because stones sink before any player can react.
argument.claim: Fairness is a number in a state machine: the warning time decides who can cross, not the chance itself.

chapters.debt: Chance returns as fate: the seed is the same for everyone, the reaction time is not. A state machine is a list of allowed states, and what it cannot name it cannot do (c8's 'the enum as allowed identities').

chapters.title: Pendulum, circle, spiral: time laid into space
chapters.body: A pendulum sampled in _physics_process into a bounded queue and laid out in space as one MultiMesh of marks, so the swing's time becomes a sculpture; then the same runner at (cos t, sin t), a circle; then the radius changes each turn, a spiral starting at 0.5 m.

argument.axis: radius change per turn (still at the tenth turn)
argument.predict: -0.2 and -0.05 will look most alike: both have died into the centre by the tenth turn (-0.2 after two and a half turns, -0.05 exactly at the tenth). 0 is the only closed form; the growing ones differ only in how wide they open.
argument.claim: The sign of one number decides whether the form lives or dies: Klee's lengthening radius makes a 'vibrant spiral', the shortening one 'dies suddenly in the static center'.

chapters.debt: A MultiMesh draws thousands of marks in one call and pays in flexibility: every mark shares one mesh and one material. The queue forgets: the sculpture is only the last N samples. And a pendulum that returns forever is an idealisation (the damping you left out).

chapters.body: Two tones rendered sample by sample into an AudioStreamWAV (a PackedByteArray), played from an AudioStreamPlayer3D inside an Area3D you walk into; the same two sines drawn as a Lissajous figure in a MultiMesh, so the chord is also a body.

chapters.title: A colour has many faces
chapters.body: A wall of steps between two complementary colours, lerped in RGB and in HSV side by side; a flashlight whose light colour you carry changes what the wall's colours look like (Albers: one colour made to look like two).

argument.axis: the space the same two complementaries are mixed in
argument.predict: RGB and linear-light RGB will look most alike: both pass through a grey middle, Klee's central grey, and differ only in where the grey falls. HSV swings round through the hues in between and never reaches grey.
argument.claim: The middle between two colours is not in the colours but in the space you mix them in: RGB finds Klee's central grey, HSV walks around it.

chapters.title: Rules in time: cellular automata
chapters.body: An elementary automaton whose rows stack upward as walkable floor (CA_GameOfLife's history turned into collidable cells), read from one buffer and written to another; the same double-buffer step then drives Turing's reaction-diffusion on a floor you stand on.

argument.axis: the rule number, from one live cell
argument.predict: 90 and 250 will look most alike: both grow a symmetric triangle at the same speed, 90 as Sierpinski's nested holes and 250 as a regular checker. 30 and 110 are both lopsided: 30 is disorderly on one side, 110 grows toward one side only.
argument.claim: A rule of eight bits decides between order, fractal and chaos, and you cannot read which from the rule, only from running it.

chapters.debt: A CA is a grid that must end: the edges wrap or die, and the choice shows at the floor's border. Rule 30's 'randomness' is fully determined (it has been used as a random generator): pseudo-randomness returns. Reaction-diffusion is Turing's 1952 morphogenesis, the application's embodied throughline: 'can twisted rooms transcend power?' (Queer 3D).

chapters.title: The tree and its mad branch: recursion
chapters.body: A tree that calls itself: branch(depth, length, frame) draws one segment and calls branch twice with a shorter length and a turned frame, until a depth limit stops it; one seeded 'mad branch' breaks the symmetry.

argument.axis: depth limit
argument.predict: 9 and 12 will look most alike at 3 m: with a 1 m trunk and a length ratio of 0.67, the twigs added past depth 9 are under 2 cm and merge into the crown, while 12 costs eight times the segments (2^12 against 2^9).
argument.claim: Recursion must be stopped, and past some depth it only costs: the stop is a design decision the tree cannot make for itself.

chapters.debt: 'Recursion must always be controlled' (Queer 3D): an unstopped recursion is a stack overflow, the engine's refusal. The fractal is an idealisation: real trees stop for reasons (light, weight, damage), and the depth limit is where the model's honesty lives.
chapters.place: Walk under the crown; climb the first branches (colliders on the thick segments only, which is another budget).

chapters.title: How do we navigate an auto-generated world?

chapters.title: Bodies that learn: whose data trains the body
chapters.body: A classifier painted on the floor: labelled points (your ch6 walk traces and classmates', with consent, loaded from a JSON file that records who labelled each one) and a k-nearest-neighbour rule that colours every floor cell by its nearest labels; then a perceptron's line on the same data, and a gradient landscape you walk down.

argument.claim: The decision field is a map of who labelled the data: the machine's confidence is borrowed from its labellers.

The course's own AI assistant (ch8) was trained on labels nobody in the room chose: ask it for 'a human body' and study what it returns. A test proves only what you thought to ask: the perceptron fails XOR.

chapters.title: Order toward entropy: the QFEP laboratory
chapters.body: Your own prediction log becomes a body: every prediction and observation you wrote since ch2, loaded from your sketchbook, with F = |prediction - observation| per chapter drawn as a line you walk along (QFEP's F term). Beside it, 200 seeded symbols sorted by a tween while their Shannon entropy is counted (Random_Entropy).

argument.axis: how the same 200 symbols are arranged
argument.predict: 'sorted by value' and 'reversed' will look most alike: they are mirror images. All four carry exactly the same counted entropy: the picture changes and the number does not.
argument.claim: Entropy counts what there is, not how it is arranged: order is a picture, not a quantity.

chapters.debt: Shannon entropy measures a distribution and is blind to arrangement: the metric hides exactly what a visual argument shows. QFEP is the project's own framework, and the F term measured on the course's learners must not become a score (c2's warning): the log is for the student, not for the grade.

What no comparable course has, and the course says so plainly [V LEARN]: bodies in 3D and VR that a person stands on, carries or becomes; a falsifiable prediction of the closest pair before every render; and a geometric and topological queering (polycount against deformation, the blob, the recursion that must be stopped, impossible space) that the critical-code canon, whose critique is social and linguistic, does not yet cover.
